SIL Global  
Formation 1934;92 years ago  
Type Scientific institute  
Purpose Research in linguistics, promotion of literacy, language preservation, Bible translation  
HeadquartersDallas, Texas, United States  
FounderWilliam Cameron Townsend  
Executive director Johnstone Ndunde[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
Board chair Hans Combrink[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
AffiliationsEvangelical Christianity  
Websitewww.sil.org  
Formerly called Summer Institute of Linguistics
**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.
texts.1:
William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.
texts.2:
### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.
texts.3:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)
texts.4:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)
texts.5:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

##### Serving the world’s language communities since 1934.


#### SIL Global is a community of local organizations that partner with minority language communities to help them use their languages to know God, learn freely, and live with dignity.
Many people around the world face hardship and discrimination because of the languages they speak or sign. We walk alongside 1,572 language communities in 119 countries to help turn those barriers of exclusion into bridges for flourishing.

## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### VISION
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.

## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### MISSION
Inspired by God’s love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.

## Our Why
Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.
As followers of Jesus, we believe:
*   All people are important.That’s why we care about all languages.  
*   Relationship with God is precious.That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.  
*   All aspects of a person’s life matter.That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.

## Our Leadership
*   ### Meet Our
Executive Director
**Dr. Johnstone Ndunde** became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025, bringing 20 years of leadership in Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, with a strong focus on collaboration, education, and flourishing language communities.

## Our Leadership
###### Meet More Leaders
See the profiles of our leadership staff.

## Our History
#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
In 1917, a young American named Cameron Townsend traveled through Guatemala selling Spanish Bibles. He soon realized that the indigenous people couldn’t use his Bibles – they didn’t speak Spanish. He also saw that they were oppressed in ways that affected all parts of their lives: their faith, language, social standing, and economic health.
Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics in 1934 as a summer training program for linguists to work with local people like those in Guatemala. Today we are SIL Global, a multicultural community of local organizations working with over 1,500 language communities throughout the world.

## Our History
#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
##### 1930s
Cameron Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics to serve language communities on the margins of society.
More and more students came to study linguistics and went on to work in Mexico.

Title: SIL Global

"Summer Institute of Linguistics" redirects here. For the Linguistic Society of America's Summer Linguistics Institute, see Linguistic Society of America.
SIL Global  
Formation 1934;92 years ago  
Type Scientific institute  
Purpose Research in linguistics, promotion of literacy, language preservation, Bible translation  
HeadquartersDallas, Texas, United States  
FounderWilliam Cameron Townsend  
Executive director Johnstone Ndunde[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
Board chair Hans Combrink[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
AffiliationsEvangelical Christianity  
Websitewww.sil.org  
Formerly called Summer Institute of Linguistics
**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

## Methodological contributions
[edit]

texts.0: ##### Serving the world’s language communities since 1934.
texts.1:
#### SIL Global is a community of local organizations that partner with minority language communities to help them use their languages to know God, learn freely, and live with dignity.
Many people around the world face hardship and discrimination because of the languages they speak or sign. We walk alongside 1,572 language communities in 119 countries to help turn those barriers of exclusion into bridges for flourishing.
texts.2:
## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### VISION
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.
texts.3:
## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### MISSION
Inspired by God’s love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.
texts.4:
## Our Why
Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.
As followers of Jesus, we believe:
*   All people are important.That’s why we care about all languages.  
*   Relationship with God is precious.That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.  
*   All aspects of a person’s life matter.That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.
texts.5:
## Our Leadership
*   ### Meet Our
Executive Director
**Dr. Johnstone Ndunde** became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025, bringing 20 years of leadership in Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, with a strong focus on collaboration, education, and flourishing language communities.
texts.6:
## Our Leadership
###### Meet More Leaders
See the profiles of our leadership staff.
texts.7:
## Our History
#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
In 1917, a young American named Cameron Townsend traveled through Guatemala selling Spanish Bibles. He soon realized that the indigenous people couldn’t use his Bibles – they didn’t speak Spanish. He also saw that they were oppressed in ways that affected all parts of their lives: their faith, language, social standing, and economic health.
Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics in 1934 as a summer training program for linguists to work with local people like those in Guatemala. Today we are SIL Global, a multicultural community of local organizations working with over 1,500 language communities throughout the world.

#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
##### 1930s
Cameron Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics to serve language communities on the margins of society.
More and more students came to study linguistics and went on to work in Mexico.

##### Serving the world’s language communities since 1934.


#### SIL Global is a community of local organizations that partner with minority language communities to help them use their languages to know God, learn freely, and live with dignity.
Many people around the world face hardship and discrimination because of the languages they speak or sign. We walk alongside 1,572 language communities in 119 countries to help turn those barriers of exclusion into bridges for flourishing.

## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### VISION
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.

## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### MISSION
Inspired by God’s love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.

## Our Why
Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.
As followers of Jesus, we believe:
*   All people are important.That’s why we care about all languages.  
*   Relationship with God is precious.That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.  
*   All aspects of a person’s life matter.That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.

## Our Leadership
*   ### Meet Our
Executive Director
**Dr. Johnstone Ndunde** became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025, bringing 20 years of leadership in Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, with a strong focus on collaboration, education, and flourishing language communities.

## Our Leadership
###### Meet More Leaders
See the profiles of our leadership staff.

## Our History
#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
In 1917, a young American named Cameron Townsend traveled through Guatemala selling Spanish Bibles. He soon realized that the indigenous people couldn’t use his Bibles – they didn’t speak Spanish. He also saw that they were oppressed in ways that affected all parts of their lives: their faith, language, social standing, and economic health.
Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics in 1934 as a summer training program for linguists to work with local people like those in Guatemala. Today we are SIL Global, a multicultural community of local organizations working with over 1,500 language communities throughout the world.

## Our History
#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
##### 1930s
Cameron Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics to serve language communities on the margins of society.
More and more students came to study linguistics and went on to work in Mexico.

## Purpose
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.
SIL's service with ethnolinguistic minority communities is motivated by the belief that all people are created in the image of God, and that languages and cultures are part of the richness of God's creation. SIL is founded on the principle that communities should be able to pursue their social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual goals without sacrificing their ethnolinguistic identity. As a faith-based nonprofit organization, SIL works alongside language communities as they discover how to harness the power of their language to address challenges and reach their goals.

Formerly called Summer Institute of Linguistics
**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

"Summer Institute of Linguistics" redirects here. For the Linguistic Society of America's Summer Linguistics Institute, see Linguistic Society of America.
SIL Global  
Formation 1934;92 years ago  
Type Scientific institute  
Purpose Research in linguistics, promotion of literacy, language preservation, Bible translation  
HeadquartersDallas, Texas, United States  
FounderWilliam Cameron Townsend  
Executive director Johnstone Ndunde[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
Board chair Hans Combrink[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
AffiliationsEvangelical Christianity  
Websitewww.sil.org  
Formerly called Summer Institute of Linguistics
**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.
texts.1:
William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.
texts.2:
### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.
texts.3:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)
texts.4:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)
texts.5:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

texts.0: ##### Serving the world’s language communities since 1934.
texts.1:
#### SIL Global is a community of local organizations that partner with minority language communities to help them use their languages to know God, learn freely, and live with dignity.
Many people around the world face hardship and discrimination because of the languages they speak or sign. We walk alongside 1,572 language communities in 119 countries to help turn those barriers of exclusion into bridges for flourishing.
texts.2:
## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### VISION
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.
texts.3:
## Our Vision & Mission
#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**
###### MISSION
Inspired by God’s love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.
texts.4:
## Our Why
Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.
As followers of Jesus, we believe:
*   All people are important.That’s why we care about all languages.  
*   Relationship with God is precious.That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.  
*   All aspects of a person’s life matter.That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.
texts.5:
## Our Leadership
*   ### Meet Our
Executive Director
**Dr. Johnstone Ndunde** became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025, bringing 20 years of leadership in Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, with a strong focus on collaboration, education, and flourishing language communities.

See the profiles of our leadership staff.
texts.7:
## Our History
#### People & Language. For over 90 years.
In 1917, a young American named Cameron Townsend traveled through Guatemala selling Spanish Bibles. He soon realized that the indigenous people couldn’t use his Bibles – they didn’t speak Spanish. He also saw that they were oppressed in ways that affected all parts of their lives: their faith, language, social standing, and economic health.
Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics in 1934 as a summer training program for linguists to work with local people like those in Guatemala. Today we are SIL Global, a multicultural community of local organizations working with over 1,500 language communities throughout the world.

More and more students came to study linguistics and went on to work in Mexico.

## Summary
We are a global, faith-based nonprofit that works with local communities around the world to develop language solutions that expand possibilities for a better life. SIL's core contribution areas are Bible translation, literacy, education, development, linguistic research and language tools.
We are eager for the day when all people enjoy equal access to education, to socio-economic opportunities, and to resources for spiritual growth - no matter what language they speak or sign.

## Purpose
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.
SIL's service with ethnolinguistic minority communities is motivated by the belief that all people are created in the image of God, and that languages and cultures are part of the richness of God's creation. SIL is founded on the principle that communities should be able to pursue their social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual goals without sacrificing their ethnolinguistic identity. As a faith-based nonprofit organization, SIL works alongside language communities as they discover how to harness the power of their language to address challenges and reach their goals.

Title: SIL Global
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
"Summer Institute of Linguistics" redirects here. For the Linguistic Society of America's Summer Linguistics Institute, see Linguistic Society of America.
SIL Global  
Formation 1934;92 years ago  
Type Scientific institute  
Purpose Research in linguistics, promotion of literacy, language preservation, Bible translation  
HeadquartersDallas, Texas, United States  
FounderWilliam Cameron Townsend  
Executive director Johnstone Ndunde[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
Board chair Hans Combrink[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
AffiliationsEvangelical Christianity  
Websitewww.sil.org  
Formerly called Summer Institute of Linguistics
**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

## Methodological contributions
[edit]

Source: https://www.sil.org/translation/what-we-do
Title: What we do
Chunks: 0
Translation in SIL focuses on:
*   Partnership with language communities around the world;  
*   Training programs, both formal and informal;  
*   Technical services, providing publications and consultant assistance for translators; and,  
*   Research and development in translation theory and practice.
SIL is currently involved in various aspects of translation work in partnership with speakers of more than 1,000 languages around the world. The diverse ethnolinguistic contexts in which SIL works require a scholarly approach to translation based on current translation theory. Wherever possible, SIL seeks to work with national and international translation organizations in cooperative efforts to provide the necessary training, and technical and consultant services needed in each situation.

**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.
texts.1:
William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.
texts.2:
### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.
texts.3:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)
texts.4:
### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

## History
The principal founder of SIL International was William Cameron Townsend (1896-1982). He began cross-cultural work with the Kaqchikel people of Guatemala in 1919. By 1929, Townsend's vision had broadened to include other peoples who also needed language development. SIL International (then known as the Summer Institute of Linguistics) began in 1934 as a summer training program in Arkansas, USA, with two students. The enrollment of these summer classes grew each subsequent year.
Kenneth L. Pike (1912-2000) was one of five students in the 1935 course. He began work on the Mixtec language in the state of Oaxaca, Mexico. This work launched Pike into his life-long work in linguistics and the study of language in the context of human behavior. Dr. Pike served as President of SIL until 1979.
For a timeline, visit: sil.org/about/history
* * *

## Program accomplishments
As of October 2021, we are involved in approximately 1,633 active language projects in 98 countries. These projects impact more than 855+ million people within 1,347 local communities. SIL's work brings together more than 4,200 staff from 84 countries who work alongside thousands more local partners and community volunteers worldwide.

languages, a relative newcomer. Of  great importance is that English has been recorded

texts.21:
## [PDF page 7]
If  the  rise  of  post- Structuralist  modern  linguistics  can  be  dated  to  the  publication  of  
Noam  Chomsky ’s  Syntactic  Structures  in  1957,  developments  within  and  discoveries  
in  historical  linguistics  have  since  the  mid-  20th  century   –  notably  the  Laryngeal  theory  
(see  Chapter   2)   –  greatly  refined  our  ability  to  describe  language  change  and  the  envi-  
ronment  for  changes  in  the  sounds,  inflections,  syntax,  and  vocabulary  (both  lexis,  the  
total  set  of  words  that  comprise  the  vocabulary,  and  semantics,  the  meanings  of  those  
words)  of  a  language.  The  development  of  sociolinguistics  has  re -  focused  attention  on  
the  broader  environment  of  language  development:  the  nature  of  speech  communities  
and social networks, the role of  class, ethnicity, gender, even religion in linguistic social  
stratification. The rise of  pidgin and Creole studies, that is, the study of  language contact  
varieties  such  as  the  English-  based  varieties  of  the  Caribbean  and  Pacific  Islands,  has  
given  valuable  insight  into  the  language  contact  situations  that  produce  change  (such  
as  loan  formations  or  inflectional  changes)  or  give  birth  to  wholly  new  varieties  that  
can  serve  as  the  L1  of  a  speech  community  (Creoles),  besides  the  insight  gleaned  with  
regard  to  child  language  development  and  language  acquisition.  And  the  refinement  
of  linguistic  taxonomy   –  one  of  the  signal  advances  in  linguistic  knowledge  of  the  
Enlightenment –  allows us to begin to ground the analysis of  English in specifics.

## [PDF page 8]
The  English  language  is  an  Indo-  European  language,  and  while  this  is  a  subject  
reserved  for  more  detail  in  the  following  chapter,  it  needs  to  be  said  at  the  outset  
that  this  ‘taxonomic’  classification  has  significant  entailments.  While  the  ‘genetic  
classification’ of  human languages involves some metaphorical abstraction, nonethe -  
less,  one  can  think  of  human  languages  as  having  ‘heritable’  features  and  of  more  
closely ‘related’ languages sharing in common more core features (in sounds, grammar,  
syntax, and vocabulary) than those less closely related. Thus historical linguists speak  
of  ‘parent’  and  ‘daughter ’  languages.  For  English,  the  genetic  classification  is  Indo-  
European, Germanic, West Germanic, in terms of  its super- or macro-  family, branch,  
and  subbranch relationships (the particular terms for groupings of  related languages  
as used in family-  tree diagrams can vary slightly). West Germanic comprises German,  
Yiddish,  Dutch,  Afrikaans,  Frisian,  and  English;  Yiddish  (from  German  Jüdisch,  
i.e.,  ‘Jewish’  German  contact  variety  of  German  and  Hebrew)  and  Afrikaans  (from  
Dutch  Afrikaansch  ‘African,’  also  called  ‘the  Taal’  or  Cape  Dutch  contact  variety  of  
Dutch,  English,  Zulu,  Xhosa,  and  other  African  languages)  are  Creoles  often  given  
in  a  listing  of  West  Germanic  languages  –  somewhat  unusually  for  contact  language  
varieties,  they  have  historically  been  written  down, Yiddish  in  particular  with  a  rich  
literature  of  its  own.  Germanic  is  comprised  of  two  living  branches  and  one  extinct
texts.25:
## [PDF page 8]
branch:  West  Germanic,  North  Germanic  (Greenlandic,  Icelandic,  Faroese,  Norn  
[now  extinct,  formerly  spoken  on  Shetland  and  the  Orkneys  and  parts  of  Northern  
Scotland],  Norwegian,  Swedish,  and  Danish),  and  East  Germanic  (an  extinct  branch  
including  Gothic,  of  which  we  have  the  translation  of  Greek  Scripture  by  Ulfilas,  
and  likely Vandalic  [Hartmann  2020],  a  line  of  which  may  be  preserved  in  the  Latin  
Anthology  in  addition  to  some  personal  names  in  classical  sources,  Burgundian,  and  
Crimean Gothic). The relative relatedness of  Germanic to other branches in the Indo-  
European macro-  family of  languages is a matter of  continued debate, but there seems  
to  be  a  good  case  for  some  degree  of  closer  affiliation  to  Baltic  (see  Chapter   2).  At  
the  super-  or  macro-  family  level,  English  is  part  of  a  family  of  languages  spanning,  
in  the  pre - colonial  period,  Western  Europe  to  South  Asia;  perhaps  half  the  world’s  
population  speaks  an  Indo-  European  tongue  as  a  first  or  second  language,  in  large  
part due to the numbers of  speakers of  such IE languages as English, Hindi, Spanish,  
Russian, and French.  
The entire notion of  ‘relatedness’ among languages relies upon a good number of  
theoretical  underpinnings;  for  the  moment,  one  presumption  involves  the  ultimate  
unitary  phenomenon  that  is  human  language:  that  all  human  languages,  living  and  
recorded, derive from an original Ur-  language, that they all share linguistic universals

## History
The principal founder of SIL International was William Cameron Townsend (1896-1982). He began cross-cultural work with the Kaqchikel people of Guatemala in 1919. By 1929, Townsend's vision had broadened to include other peoples who also needed language development. SIL International (then known as the Summer Institute of Linguistics) began in 1934 as a summer training program in Arkansas, USA, with two students. The enrollment of these summer classes grew each subsequent year.
Kenneth L. Pike (1912-2000) was one of five students in the 1935 course. He began work on the Mixtec language in the state of Oaxaca, Mexico. This work launched Pike into his life-long work in linguistics and the study of language in the context of human behavior. Dr. Pike served as President of SIL until 1979.
For a timeline, visit: sil.org/about/history

## Program accomplishments
As of October 2021, we are involved in approximately 1,633 active language projects in 98 countries. These projects impact more than 855+ million people within 1,347 local communities. SIL's work brings together more than 4,200 staff from 84 countries who work alongside thousands more local partners and community volunteers worldwide.
